Vignette:
# Mariana's Case

Mariana was thirty-four when she first came to the prison intake office, a job she had held for six years without incident. What no one at the facility knew—what she had never told her supervisor or her husband, David—was that every time she put on her uniform in the dark of their bedroom, she felt the fabric like a second skin she could not shed. The navy shirt, the badge, the belt: they were armor she needed and armor that terrified her.

The work itself had become a minefield. Two months before seeking help, Mariana had been standing in the processing area when Lieutenant Gomez approached with a routine instruction about prisoner intake forms. The moment his voice took on that tone—firm, authoritative, the unmistakable cadence of command—her body had gone rigid. Her hands had begun to shake. She had excused herself to the bathroom and sat in a stall for twenty minutes, her heart hammering, trying to remember that she was safe, that she was the one in uniform now, that she was in control. But she was not in control. Not of her body. Not of the way her mind had split open.

The traumatic event itself belonged to a different lifetime, or so Mariana had tried to convince herself. She had been nineteen, living in Guatemala City with her mother and younger brother. Her father, a man who drank heavily and unpredictably, had come home one evening in a rage—the kind that made the house itself seem to hold its breath. He had been drinking, and the smell of it, that particular sharp-sweet stench of cheap rum mixed with sweat and anger, had filled the kitchen where Mariana and her brother were eating. Her mother had tried to intervene when their father began shouting at Mariana's brother, accusing him of stealing money. The argument had escalated. There had been violence—her father's fists, her mother's screams, the sound of her brother being thrown against the wall. Mariana had frozen, unable to move, unable to speak, watching as a man she had once loved became a force of pure destruction. The police had come eventually, summoned by a neighbor. The officers in their uniforms, their voices sharp with authority, their presence somehow both a rescue and a re-traumatization—the sense that even rescue could arrive as a threat.

Her mother had died from her injuries three days later. Mariana and her brother had been taken in by their grandmother, and within two years, the family had applied for refugee status. The asylum process had taken four more years. Mariana had spent that time waiting, watching, learning that the world operated on a logic she could no longer trust. People in power—immigration officials, judges, bureaucrats—held her fate in their hands. She had learned to be small, to anticipate danger, to believe that safety was conditional and always threatened.

By the time she was hired as a prison guard, Mariana had rebuilt a life. She had married David, a kind man who worked in construction, who asked few questions about her silences. She had a salary, health insurance, a house with a mortgage. But the job, which should have represented stability and authority on her side of the divide, had instead become a daily collision with her past.

The triggers had woven themselves into her workday. Every time a supervisor gave her an instruction, her nervous system interpreted it as imminent danger. The smell of alcohol—which sometimes clung to inmates or occasionally to a guard who had come in after a long night—would send her spiraling into a state of hypervigilance that could last for hours. And uniforms, the very thing she wore, seemed to activate a cascade of fear. She had come to believe that authority itself was fundamentally corrupting, that people in power—even herself—were capable of violence at any moment.

Over the past three months, Mariana's coping mechanisms had calcified into habits that were slowly dismantling her life. She had taken to playing loud reggaeton music in her car during her commute, the volume so high it drowned out her thoughts, but also meant she could not hear if someone was trying to speak to her. At work, she had begun to position herself strategically in rooms, always choosing a seat where she could see all exits, where she felt least exposed. Her coworkers had noticed her withdrawal. David had noticed her flinching at unexpected sounds, the way she would sometimes go rigid if he moved too quickly toward her in the dark.

The memories themselves were crystalline and unbearable. When they surfaced—and they surfaced without warning—Mariana did not simply remember the event; she heard it. She heard her brother's cry, her mother's voice, the wet sound of impact, the police sirens wailing through the neighborhood. The sensory detail was so acute that her body could not distinguish between remembering and reliving. When a memory arrived, the emotional overwhelm was so complete that she would have to stop whatever she was doing—sometimes in the middle of a shift—and wait for it to pass.

What had finally brought Mariana to the clinic was a moment of reckoning. She had overreacted to a false alarm on the unit—a dropped tray that sounded like a weapon—and had drawn her baton before she understood what had happened. A younger officer had looked at her with something like fear. That night, David had asked her if she was okay, and she had realized that she could not answer honestly without telling him everything, and she could not tell him everything without admitting that the woman he had married was slowly disappearing. She was afraid of what she was becoming. She was hoping that someone could help her separate the past from the present, the threat that had been real from the threats her mind continued to manufacture. She was hoping, though she barely dared to articulate it, that she might one day wear her uniform without feeling like she was wearing her father's violence.
